title: The carob tree (Taanit 23a)
hook: an old man plants a tree he'll never eat from, for his grandchildren

segments.voice: Yesterday Honi drew a circle and wouldn't step out until the rain came. Your line was draw the circle. Did you ask for something without shrinking it? Day two hundred seventy-eight.

Somebody planted the big tree on your street. Somebody laid the stones of the oldest building in your town, dug the well, started the library, wrote down the recipe your family still makes. Most of them never saw you. They never knew your name. They just did the work and left it for whoever came next. The Talmud tells a story about Honi, the circle-drawer, walking down a road and meeting one of those people. A man, planting a tree.
screen: `WHO PLANTED YOUR STREET'S TREE?` → `THEY NEVER KNEW YOUR NAME.` → `A MAN, PLANTING.`

segments.voice: It's the same page of tractate Taanit as yesterday's circle, and you met this scene once before, back with Rabbi Tarfon, as a picture of work you won't finish. Today, look closer. Honi is on a road and sees a man planting a carob tree. Retellings usually make him old; the Talmud just says a certain man. Honi asks: how long until this tree gives fruit? Seventy years, the man says. Honi presses him: are you sure you'll live another seventy years? Now listen to the order of the answer. He doesn't start with the future. He starts with what he found. I found the world with carob trees in it. Just as my ancestors planted for me, I'm planting for my children. First he looks back and notices a gift. Then he looks forward and passes it on. The planting grows out of the noticing. In the Psalms, seventy years is a full life, so the man is planting past the edge of his own, on purpose. The story keeps going from here, and Honi's next seventy years will surprise him. We'll come back to that. For today, stay with the word found. It's a small picture of how a tradition works at all. Every teaching you've heard on this path, somebody planted. They memorized it, copied it, argued over it, carried it through exile, and passed it down to people they'd never meet. Including you.
screen: `HOW LONG UNTIL IT BEARS FRUIT?` · `FIRST, WHAT HE FOUND.` · `THEN, WHAT HE PASSES ON.` · `A TRADITION IS PLANTED TOO.` · then, large: `PLANT FOR OTHERS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find your carob trees, then plant one. Settle, and breathe. Look around wherever you are. Name three things in reach that someone made or planted before you ever arrived. A chair, a road, a word you use. Say thank you, silently, to people you'll never meet. Now think of one small thing you could start today that someone else will enjoy after you. A seed in a pot. A note in a book. Teaching a kid a family recipe. The bell holds the time.
The carob tree. A man plants one that won't bear fruit for seventy years, because his ancestors planted for him.
Your line: plant for others. Today, start one small thing that someone after you will get to enjoy. Day two hundred seventy-eight.

screen: `DAY 278 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THIS TOO IS FOR GOOD.`

howItsDone: The carob story is often told on Tu BiShvat, the new year of trees, when some Jews plant trees or eat fruits such as carob.

fork.setup: you're planting a tree that won't fruit for seventy years. a stranger asks: will you live to eat from it? what do you say first?
options: I found carob trees here, so I plant for my children.
fork.reveal: he started with what he'd found: I found the world with carob trees. as my ancestors planted for me, I plant for my children.

original.note: Hebrew: carob, the slow tree in the story.

trapdoor: what you thought: a nice story about gardening.
what it means: you eat from what others planted, so you plant for those who come after.
what a scholar hears: the seventy years echoes Psalm 90's span of a life, and it sets up Honi's own seventy-year sleep in the same passage.

notes: Editor review (2026-10-01): day 264 already told this exact story (Honi, the carob, 'my ancestors planted for me'); the teach now names that and takes a new angle (the answer starts with what he found, gratitude before planting); the Talmud says 'a certain man', not an old man, so voice, games and fork no longer call him old (the index hook still says 'old man' and 'grandchildren'; suggest the outline say 'a man' and 'children'); new myth item replaces one that repeated day 264; stock line 'an answer people have been repeating ever since' cut; howItsDone 'favorite' and 'many Jews' softened.
Taanit 23a paraphrased. Honi's seventy-year sleep follows in the same passage and is taught on day 286; the script only hints at it.

Seventy years for a carob to fruit is the story's number; real carob trees bear within several years to about a decade. The script says carob is 'slow' and 'takes years' and avoids claiming seventy is literal.
Psalm 90:10 (the days of our years are threescore years and ten) is paraphrased as 'seventy years is a whole human life'.
Tu BiShvat custom of eating carob (bokser) is common in Ashkenazi communities; check phrasing.
